scenes.title: The Uncertainty Principle
scenes.subtitle: Why nature sets a hard limit on what we can know

narration.text: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle says position and momentum cannot both be known precisely. This is not bad instrumentation. It is how nature works.

scenes.definition: Measuring a particle's position more sharply always widens the spread of its momentum, and vice versa.

narration.text: The more precisely you measure position, the less precisely you can know momentum. The limit is intrinsic, rooted in the wave nature of matter.

scenes.heading: What the rule says
items: Sharper position means wider momentum spread
The product has a hard floor: Planck's constant over four pi
It applies to every conjugate pair, not just this one

narration.text: Measuring position more sharply widens the momentum spread. The product of the two uncertainties has a hard floor, Planck's constant over four pi. And the rule applies to every conjugate pair.
The principle sets the scale of atoms. Electrons cannot fall into the nucleus, because that would pin down position and momentum at once. Chemistry itself follows from this rule.

scenes.text: What we observe is not nature itself, but nature exposed to our method of questioning.

narration.text: As Heisenberg himself put it, what we observe is not nature itself, but nature exposed to our method of questioning.
